title: With hardship, ease
hook: with every hardship comes ease, said twice

segments.voice: Yesterday: Paul's thorn, asked away three times, and still there. Your line was strength in weakness. Did you let someone help? Today the theme of suffering moves to the Quran, and a short chapter with a line said twice. Day seven hundred nineteen.

"But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall's English, translating two short verses of the Quran. Read it slowly and something odd happens. The second line adds nothing new. Apart from the 'but' that opens the first, it's the same words in the same order. In an essay, you'd cut it. And yet there it is, said again, the way you'd say something twice to a friend who didn't quite hear you the first time. Or didn't quite believe it. Today, the chapter those lines come from, and why the repeat matters.
screen: `WITH HARDSHIP GOETH EASE.` → `SAID AGAIN, ALMOST WORD FOR WORD.` → `WHY SAY IT TWICE?`

segments.voice: First, the chapter. It's one of the short ones near the end of the Quran, called the Expansion, or the Opening Up. Tradition says it came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a hard time. It begins with questions: did God not open up your chest, and lift from you the burden that weighed down your back? Before any promise, it remembers relief that has already come. Second, the small word. Pickthall doesn't write after hardship. He writes with hardship. The ease isn't only waiting at the far end of the road. It walks alongside the hard thing, already present in it, even when it's hard to see. Third, the repeat. The line comes twice. Some readers hear it as emphasis, the way a person repeats what matters. Some commentators go further: they read the twice-said line as one hardship met by two eases. Either way, the chapter won't let the reassurance be said only once. Fourth, what comes after. The chapter doesn't end in comfort and a nap. Its closing verses turn to work and to God: when you're free of one task, keep at the next, and turn your longing to your Lord. Ease, in this reading, isn't escape from life. It's what makes it possible to keep going inside it.
screen: `A CHAPTER THAT REMEMBERS RELIEF.` · `WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `SAID TWICE: TWO EASES?` · `THEN, BACK TO WORK.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one hardship you're carrying right now. Don't argue with it; just let it be there. Now look inside it, not after it, for one ease. Something small that's with you in it. A person who checks in. A warm meal. A moment when the worry went quiet. A strength you didn't know you had. When you find one, rest your attention there for a few breaths. Then the hardship, then the ease again. Both are here. The bell holds the time.
With hardship: the opening of a line the Quran says twice, with hardship goeth ease. With, not after. Today's word.
Your line: with hardship, ease. Today, when something hard comes, look for one ease already inside it, and name it to yourself. Say it twice if you need to. Day seven hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims may recite this chapter in prayer, and some say its line about hardship and ease to one another in difficult times.

fork.setup: you're writing down a promise of comfort for someone in a hard time. you've said it once. what does this chapter do?
options: move on to the next point.
add a warning in case it doesn't come true.
fork.reveal: the Quran says it twice: "with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." some commentators read the repeat as two eases for one hardship.

original.note: Arabic, Quran 94:6: truly, with hardship is ease. 'usr is hardship; yusr is ease.

trapdoor: what you thought: things get better eventually.
what it means: the Quran says ease comes with hardship, not only after it, and says so twice.
what a scholar hears: Surah al-Sharh (94), verses 5–6; some commentators read the definite 'the hardship' and the indefinite 'ease' as one hardship met by two eases.

sources.quoted: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease.

notes: Confirm Pickthall's exact wording and punctuation of 94:5–6.

Editor: 'Muslims understand it as addressed to the Prophet' changed to 'tradition says' (the occasion is not in the surah); cut the uncited Arabic-grammar claim from voice and the sweeping 'Muslims hold these readings side by side'; kept the two-eases reading attributed to 'some commentators'.
Surah names: al-Sharh / al-Inshirah, rendered in voice as 'the Expansion, or the Opening Up'; confirm the English glosses.
'Muslims understand it as addressed to the Prophet at a hard time': confirm phrasing; the occasion is from the tafsir tradition, not stated in the surah.
'One of the short ones near the end of the Quran' is a placement description, not a count.

The 'one hardship, two eases' reading (al-'usr definite, yusr indefinite) is attributed to 'some commentators' (it is reported from early authorities, e.g. Ibn Abbas, in tafsir); confirm it is fair to present.
94:7–8 paraphrased ('when you're free of one task, keep at the next, and turn your longing to your Lord'); confirm.
Original transliteration and stress of 94:6; confirm. Note the script paraphrases 'truly, with hardship is ease' (not quoted).

Auditor (2026-10-01): the hook said the repeat was 'same words, same order' and the game said 'word for word', but Pickthall's 94:5 opens 'But lo!' and 94:6 does not (the Arabic likewise has fa-inna then inna); voice, hook screen, match and fork now say 'almost' / 'back to back'.
